# Bottom line

- It is unlikely that low-level asbestos exposure alone causes classic COPD with high probability, but epidemiologic and physiologic evidence indicates a measurable, modest risk of COPD (and related lung function impairment) among workers exposed to asbestos, including at low-to-moderate cumulative exposures typical of construction and maintenance work with asbestos-containing materials (ACM). <cite id="093952f1-1">In a large asbestos worker registry, COPD incidence was elevated with asbestos exposure overall (RR 1.42) and increased further with longer exposure, demonstrating a dose–response signal for COPD with asbestos exposure</cite> <cite id="093952f1-3">and a cross-sectional study found that COPD subjects with a history of asbestos exposure had increased risk even after cessation of exposure</cite> <cite id="093952f1-4">while a meta-analysis showed significant reductions in lung function (VC, FEV1, FEV1/VC) among asbestos-exposed workers even without radiographic abnormalities</cite> <cite id="093952f1-9">with Libby cohort data showing excess COPD at low cumulative exposure levels</cite>.  
- For a sheet metal worker exposed to low-to-moderate levels, the likelihood of COPD attributable to asbestos is modestly increased compared with no exposure, but substantially lower than risks for asbestos-related cancers; risk rises with heavier or longer exposure and co-exposure to smoking. <cite id="093952f1-1">In registry data that include construction and maintenance trades, longer reported asbestos exposure was associated with higher COPD risk</cite> <cite id="093952f1-6">and in downstream-user occupations (which encompass many trades including sheet metal), asbestos exposure categories were associated with COPD</cite>.

# What the evidence shows

## Epidemiologic associations and dose–response
- In Ontario's Asbestos Workers Register (AWR), which includes construction and maintenance workers, COPD incidence was elevated among those with asbestos exposure (RR 1.42, 95% CI 1.29–1.57) overall; workers with longer reported exposure (≥140 hours) had even higher risks for COPD, as well as asbestosis and cancers, indicating a dose–response pattern for COPD with asbestos exposure. <cite id="093952f1-1">Exposure to asbestos in construction and building maintenance contributes to COPD incidence, and longer exposure is linked to higher COPD risk</cite>.  
- In general population studies that include downstream users (e.g., construction trades), COPD is listed among outcomes associated with asbestos exposure categories, supporting that even indirect or lower-level occupational exposure can be linked to COPD. <cite id="093952f1-6">Jobs with higher intensities of asbestos exposure showed increased COPD risk; exploratory analyses suggest asbestos intensity relates to COPD incidence</cite>.  
- Population cohorts in Libby, Montana, where cumulative exposures can be low-to-moderate compared with mining, still showed excess COPD (SMR 2.2) and nonmalignant respiratory disease, including at cumulative exposures below commonly cited thresholds for malignancy, indicating respiratory morbidity at moderate exposure levels. <cite id="093952f1-9">There was significant excess COPD (SMR 2.2) and nonmalignant respiratory disease even among workers with <4.5 fibers/cc-years cumulative exposure</cite>.  

## Functional impairment without clear radiographic changes
- A systematic review and meta-analysis of 9,921 asbestos-exposed workers found statistically significant reductions in vital capacity (VC), FEV1, and FEV1/VC even among workers without radiological abnormalities, implying that asbestos exposure can impair lung function (including obstructive patterns) independently of classic imaging changes. <cite id="093952f1-4">Asbestos exposure is related to restrictive and obstructive lung function impairment even in the absence of radiological evidence of disease</cite>.  
- Observational data in asbestos-exposed cohorts show that individuals with past asbestos exposure can develop COPD or severe airway obstruction, consistent with functional injury from asbestos. <cite id="093952f1-3">Past asbestos exposure may increase the risk of COPD development and is associated with severe airway obstruction risk</cite>.  

## Magnitude relative to other outcomes and modifiers
- In general, COPD risk associated with asbestos is smaller than risks for asbestos-related cancers, which show strong, graded exposure–response relationships; COPD risk shows a more modest increase that still rises with exposure duration. <cite id="093952f1-1">Longer asbestos exposure was linked to increased COPD and other respiratory diseases</cite> <cite id="093952f1-9">and excess nonmalignant respiratory disease was observed at low cumulative exposures</cite>.  
- Smoking substantially amplifies COPD risk; analyses of asbestos cohorts adjust for smoking, and where available, show increased COPD risk with asbestos even after accounting for smoking, though the excess attributable to asbestos remains. <cite id="093952f1-4">The degree of lung function impairment was partly related to the proportion of smokers included in the studies</cite> <cite id="093952f1-9">and nonmalignant respiratory disease mortality was elevated even at low cumulative exposure levels</cite>.  

# Job context: sheet metal work and ACM exposure

- Sheet metal workers in construction and building maintenance are contemporary ACM-exposed occupations; epidemiologic cohorts that include such downstream users report associations between asbestos exposure categories and COPD, indicating that lower-level, job-situation exposures can contribute to COPD risk. <cite id="093952f1-6">Asbestos exposure categories among downstream users (which include many trades such as sheet metal) were associated with COPD</cite>.  
- While the Ontario registry provides an occupational perspective and shows COPD risk increases with longer exposure, it does not provide job-specific RRs for sheet metal workers alone in the retrieved snippet; however, the presence of multiple occupations across trades and the dose–response by exposure time support that asbestos exposure at low-to-moderate levels can contribute to COPD. <cite id="093952f1-1">Asbestos exposure in construction and maintenance contributes to COPD, with risk increasing with exposure duration</cite>.  

# Classification and pathology nuances

- Asbestos exposure is a recognized cause of interstitial lung diseases; in pathology, usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern occurring in workers with asbestos exposure is classified as "asbestos-related idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis," reflecting that the parenchymal pattern is interstitial fibrosis rather than chronic bronchitis/emphysema–predominant COPD. In practice, workers with asbestos exposure and airflow obstruction can still receive a COPD diagnosis, but when an UIP pattern is demonstrated, an asbestos-related fibrosis diagnosis takes precedence. <cite id="093952f1-5">Asbestos exposure can lead to pleural and interstitial changes, with structural pleural abnormalities observed even at low cumulative exposures</cite>.  

# Practical interpretation for a sheet metal worker

- For a worker with low-to-moderate asbestos exposure (e.g., handling ACM in building maintenance or retrofit), the likelihood that asbestos causes COPD is modestly increased compared with no exposure, with risk rising in proportion to cumulative exposure and co-exposures such as smoking. <cite id="093952f1-1">COPD incidence increased with asbestos exposure (RR ~1.4 overall) and was higher with longer exposure</cite> <cite id="093952f1-4">and asbestos exposure is associated with lung function impairments even without radiographic disease</cite> <cite id="093952f1-9">including excess COPD at low cumulative exposure levels in cohort data</cite>.  
- If a clinician identifies airflow obstruction with a history of asbestos exposure, COPD remains a plausible diagnosis; conversely, if an interstitial lung disease pattern (e.g., UIP) is established, it would be termed asbestos-related fibrosis rather than classic COPD. <cite id="093952f1-5">Asbestos exposure leads to characteristic structural pleural and interstitial changes, supporting the plausibility of COPD or interstitial disease depending on pathology</cite>.  

# Remaining uncertainties

- The retrieved evidence did not provide job-specific relative risks for sheet metal workers alone; risk estimates are stronger in cohorts with higher cumulative exposures and in downstream-user groups that include sheet metal work. More granular job-exposure meta-analysis data would better quantify risk at typical sheet metal exposure levels and clarify interactions with tasks and fiber types. <cite id="093952f1-6">Downstream-user cohorts support associations between asbestos exposure and COPD</cite>.  
- Some studies focus on mixed asbestos cohorts or environmental high-exposure settings (e.g., Libby), which may not fully generalize to low-level occupational exposures; nonetheless, the consistency of COPD associations across occupational cohorts and functional impairment data supports a non-zero likelihood even at lower exposures. <cite id="093952f1-9">Excess COPD and nonmalignant respiratory disease were observed at low cumulative exposure</cite> <cite id="093952f1-4">with measurable lung function deficits among exposed workers</cite>.  

# Answer to the question

- Likelihood: For a sheet metal worker with low-to-moderate asbestos exposure, asbestos can contribute to COPD, but the attributable risk is modest—elevating COPD risk above background rather than causing it with high probability. The risk increases with longer or higher cumulative exposure and is further amplified by smoking. <cite id="093952f1-1">COPD incidence increased with asbestos exposure (RR ≈1.4 overall) and rose with longer exposure</cite> <cite id="093952f1-4">with significant lung function impairment linked to asbestos exposure even without radiographic changes</cite> <cite id="093952f1-9">and excess COPD observed at low cumulative exposure levels in cohort data</cite>.  
- Practical takeaway: If you have a history of asbestos exposure as a sheet metal worker and develop airflow obstruction, COPD is a possible diagnosis; consider smoking history and exposure duration, and evaluate for interstitial lung disease patterns that may be asbestos-related and classified as "asbestos-related idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis." <cite id="093952f1-1">Elevated COPD risk with asbestos exposure is observed in occupational cohorts</cite> <cite id="093952f1-5">and asbestos exposure produces characteristic pleural/parenchymal changes that inform diagnosis</cite>.

Snippet: INTRODUCTION
Contemporary asbestos exposure occurs during construction, remediation, and maintenance involving asbestos-containing materials (ACM), as compared to the historical exposure scenarios of asbestos mining and milling. This study reports on the risk of asbestos-related diseases (ARD) among workers in the AWR.


METHODS
AWR registrants were linked probabilistically with administrative health databases (1986-2019) to identify cases of ARD including both cancer and chronic respiratory disease. Follow-up began at AWR enrollment and continued prospectively. Incidence rates were compared to the general population using standardized incidence ratios (SIRs). Associations between ACM exposure and ARD were estimated among AWR registrants using Poisson regression.


RESULTS

Title: A Meta-analysis of Asbestos and Lung Cancer: Is Better Quality Exposure Assessment Associated with Steeper Slopes of the Exposure–Response Relationships?
Snippet: Search strategy and inclusion criteria. We searched the PubMed/MEDLINE (U.S. National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA) and EMBASE (Elsevier B.V., Amsterdam, the Netherlands) databases for cohort and case-control studies published before 2010 using combinations of the following key words: amphibole, asbestos, chrysotile, lung cancer, lung neoplasm. The initial search yielded 2,826 articles, of which 1,769 were excluded upon limiting the search to English language and human studies, and we further narrowed the list to 296 upon restriction to cohort and casecontrol studies. We scrutinized the reference lists of relevant papers for additional publications. A requirement for inclusion in the meta-analysis was that the study should have analyzed the exposure-response relationships quantitatively, with more than one estimate of cumulative exposure (CE), and with excess risk expressed per fiber-years per milliliter or risk per million particles per cubic foot year. A brief note on these two exposure assessment methods: Before the 1970s, airborne asbestos levels were usually measured with the midget impinger method by trapping total airborne (including nonfibrous) dust particles and counting via light microscope (Gibbs 1994). Membrane filter-based methods replaced the midget impinger method; fibers, generally defined as structures more than 5 μm in length with an aspect ratio ≥ 3:1, are identified and counted via phase-contrast microscopy (PCM) or, more recently, with transmission electron microscopy (TEM). 

Studies on non occupational exposures were not considered eligible. Recent studies that made use of qualitative or semiquantitative exposure assessment approaches were not included in the evaluation. Snippet: Asbestos has been classified as the acknowledged carcinogen by International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). [34] However, whether asbestos is associated with the development of other cancers remains unknown. 

During the past 10 years, a growing body of meta-analysis has been widely used in epidemiology to quantitatively assess the association between asbestos exposure and cancers via statistical method. Numerous cohort studies and systematic reviews attempted to answer the question between asbestos exposure and PCa, however, the results were debatable. In present study, we quantitatively assessed the relationship of excessive exposure to asbestos with PCa risk by applying a meta-analysis technique based on 17 independent kinds of literature. 

Our results revealed an increased PCa risk among people exposed to asbestos. In another way, people exposed to asbestos have 1.22 times of suffering from PCa compared with the general population. The risk of PCa varied in people exposed to different type of asbestos. In subgroup analysis by asbestos type, we found a suggestive and significant association between asbestos type and the PCa in meta-SMR. Cohorts exposed to crocidolite and mixed asbestos showed larger SMRs than those exposed only to chrysotile asbestos, which is consistent with what Stayner et al [35] found for mesothelioma. In addition, the nonsignificant SMR based on the 4 cohorts with exposure to chrysotile asbestos only seems to confirm the results by Li et al, [36] which based on 3 studies. The exact mechanisms of asbestos exposure leading to PCa are not fully understood. The inherent characteristics of asbestos may affect its carcinogenicity, including fiber diameter and length, surface properties of the fiber as well as the fiber durability. Previous study has reported that the diameter of crocidolite fibers is the finest followed by chrysotile, amosite, and anthophyllite and it was considered the most harmful to human health. Snippet: For each of these studies, different measures of association were reported, most commonly standardized mortality ratios and in some cases relative risks (RRs) or odds ratios. Although there are fundamental differences between these types of risk measures, for the purpose of this metaanalysis, all study designs were included and all measures of association were considered estimates of the RR. 

The outcome analyzed in the meta-analysis was the slope of the exposure-response relation, often referred to as the "lung cancer potency factor" and denoted by K L in the asbestos literature. We used the widely applied U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (1986) linear RR model, RR = α(1 + K L × CE), where α is an intercept parameter representing the background rate of lung cancer and K L is the slope of increase in the RR per unit of CE to asbestos (in fiber-years per milliliter). If available, we used associations for 10-year lagged CE (six studies) to account for latency (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 1986); otherwise, we used associations with unlagged CE (13 studies). The values for K L were obtained by fitting Poisson regression models with PROC NLMIXED (version 9.2; SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA). In our primary analyses, we did not restrict the intercept (α) in the calculation of the exposure-response curve. # Bottom line

- It is unlikely that low-level asbestos exposure alone causes classic COPD with high probability, but epidemiologic and physiologic evidence indicates a measurable, modest risk of COPD (and related lung function impairment) among workers exposed to asbestos, including at low-to-moderate cumulative exposures typical of construction and maintenance work with asbestos-containing materials (ACM). <cite id="093952f1-1">In a large asbestos worker registry, COPD incidence was elevated with asbestos exposure overall (RR 1.42) and increased further with longer exposure, demonstrating a dose–response signal for COPD with asbestos exposure</cite> <cite id="093952f1-3">and a cross-sectional study found that COPD subjects with a history of asbestos exposure had increased risk even after cessation of exposure</cite> <cite id="093952f1-4">while a meta-analysis showed significant reductions in lung function (VC, FEV1, FEV1/VC) among asbestos-exposed workers even without radiographic abnormalities</cite> <cite id="093952f1-9">with Libby cohort data showing excess COPD at low cumulative exposure levels</cite>.  
- For a sheet metal worker exposed to low-to-moderate levels, the likelihood of COPD attributable to asbestos is modestly increased compared with no exposure, but substantially lower than risks for asbestos-related cancers; risk rises with heavier or longer exposure and co-exposure to smoking. <cite id="093952f1-1">In registry data that include construction and maintenance trades, longer reported asbestos exposure was associated with higher COPD risk</cite> <cite id="093952f1-6">and in downstream-user occupations (which encompass many trades including sheet metal), asbestos exposure categories were associated with COPD</cite>.

# What the evidence shows

## Epidemiologic associations and dose–response
- In Ontario's Asbestos Workers Register (AWR), which includes construction and maintenance workers, COPD incidence was elevated among those with asbestos exposure (RR 1.42, 95% CI 1.29–1.57) overall; workers with longer reported exposure (≥140 hours) had even higher risks for COPD, as well as asbestosis and cancers, indicating a dose–response pattern for COPD with asbestos exposure. <cite id="093952f1-1">Exposure to asbestos in construction and building maintenance contributes to COPD incidence, and longer exposure is linked to higher COPD risk</cite>.  
- In general population studies that include downstream users (e.g., construction trades), COPD is listed among outcomes associated with asbestos exposure categories, supporting that even indirect or lower-level occupational exposure can be linked to COPD. <cite id="093952f1-6">Jobs with higher intensities of asbestos exposure showed increased COPD risk; exploratory analyses suggest asbestos intensity relates to COPD incidence</cite>.  
- Population cohorts in Libby, Montana, where cumulative exposures can be low-to-moderate compared with mining, still showed excess COPD (SMR 2.2) and nonmalignant respiratory disease, including at cumulative exposures below commonly cited thresholds for malignancy, indicating respiratory morbidity at moderate exposure levels. <cite id="093952f1-9">There was significant excess COPD (SMR 2.2) and nonmalignant respiratory disease even among workers with <4.5 fibers/cc-years cumulative exposure</cite>.  

## Functional impairment without clear radiographic changes
- A systematic review and meta-analysis of 9,921 asbestos-exposed workers found statistically significant reductions in vital capacity (VC), FEV1, and FEV1/VC even among workers without radiological abnormalities, implying that asbestos exposure can impair lung function (including obstructive patterns) independently of classic imaging changes. <cite id="093952f1-4">Asbestos exposure is related to restrictive and obstructive lung function impairment even in the absence of radiological evidence of disease</cite>.  
- Observational data in asbestos-exposed cohorts show that individuals with past asbestos exposure can develop COPD or severe airway obstruction, consistent with functional injury from asbestos. <cite id="093952f1-3">Past asbestos exposure may increase the risk of COPD development and is associated with severe airway obstruction risk</cite>.  

## Magnitude relative to other outcomes and modifiers
- In general, COPD risk associated with asbestos is smaller than risks for asbestos-related cancers, which show strong, graded exposure–response relationships; COPD risk shows a more modest increase that still rises with exposure duration. <cite id="093952f1-1">Longer asbestos exposure was linked to increased COPD and other respiratory diseases</cite> <cite id="093952f1-9">and excess nonmalignant respiratory disease was observed at low cumulative exposures</cite>.  
- Smoking substantially amplifies COPD risk; analyses of asbestos cohorts adjust for smoking, and where available, show increased COPD risk with asbestos even after accounting for smoking, though the excess attributable to asbestos remains. <cite id="093952f1-4">The degree of lung function impairment was partly related to the proportion of smokers included in the studies</cite> <cite id="093952f1-9">and nonmalignant respiratory disease mortality was elevated even at low cumulative exposure levels</cite>.  

# Job context: sheet metal work and ACM exposure

- Sheet metal workers in construction and building maintenance are contemporary ACM-exposed occupations; epidemiologic cohorts that include such downstream users report associations between asbestos exposure categories and COPD, indicating that lower-level, job-situation exposures can contribute to COPD risk. <cite id="093952f1-6">Asbestos exposure categories among downstream users (which include many trades such as sheet metal) were associated with COPD</cite>.

# Classification and pathology nuances

- Asbestos exposure is a recognized cause of interstitial lung diseases; in pathology, usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern occurring in workers with asbestos exposure is classified as "asbestos-related idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis," reflecting that the parenchymal pattern is interstitial fibrosis rather than chronic bronchitis/emphysema–predominant COPD. In practice, workers with asbestos exposure and airflow obstruction can still receive a COPD diagnosis, but when an UIP pattern is demonstrated, an asbestos-related fibrosis diagnosis takes precedence. <cite id="093952f1-5">Asbestos exposure can lead to pleural and interstitial changes, with structural pleural abnormalities observed even at low cumulative exposures</cite>.  

# Practical interpretation for a sheet metal worker

- For a worker with low-to-moderate asbestos exposure (e.g., handling ACM in building maintenance or retrofit), the likelihood that asbestos causes COPD is modestly increased compared with no exposure, with risk rising in proportion to cumulative exposure and co-exposures such as smoking. <cite id="093952f1-1">COPD incidence increased with asbestos exposure (RR ~1.4 overall) and was higher with longer exposure</cite> <cite id="093952f1-4">and asbestos exposure is associated with lung function impairments even without radiographic disease</cite> <cite id="093952f1-9">including excess COPD at low cumulative exposure levels in cohort data</cite>.

Snippet: INTRODUCTION

The Ontario Asbestos Workers Register (AWR) was established in 1986 to track asbestos exposure among construction workers. This study reports on the risk of asbestos-related diseases (ARD) among workers in the AWR.


METHODS
AWR registrants were linked probabilistically with administrative health databases (1986-2019) to identify cases of ARD including both cancer and chronic respiratory disease. Follow-up began at AWR enrollment and continued prospectively. Incidence rates were compared to the general population using standardized incidence ratios (SIRs). Associations between ACM exposure and ARD were estimated among AWR registrants using Poisson regression.

Snippet: Search strategy and inclusion criteria. The initial search yielded 2,826 articles, of which 1,769 were excluded upon limiting the search to English language and human studies, and we further narrowed the list to 296 upon restriction to cohort and casecontrol studies. A requirement for inclusion in the meta-analysis was that the study should have analyzed the exposure-response relationships quantitatively, with more than one estimate of cumulative exposure (CE), and with excess risk expressed per fiber-years per milliliter or risk per million particles per cubic foot year. A brief note on these two exposure assessment methods: Before the 1970s, airborne asbestos levels were usually measured with the midget impinger method by trapping total airborne (including nonfibrous) dust particles and counting via light microscope (Gibbs 1994). Membrane filter-based methods replaced the midget impinger method; fibers, generally defined as structures more than 5 μm in length with an aspect ratio ≥ 3:1, are identified and counted via phase-contrast microscopy (PCM) or, more recently, with transmission electron microscopy (TEM). 

Studies on non occupational exposures were not considered eligible. Recent studies that made use of qualitative or semiquantitative exposure assessment approaches were not included in the evaluation. Using these studies, we calculated the geometric mean comparative risk of contracting mesothelioma versus ovarian cancer from the same asbestos exposures. The subjects of the EPA occupational exposure study were entirely men. 92 Since women are more susceptible to cancer from asbestos exposure, we used Lacourt's 104 findings comparing the mesothelioma odds ratio (OR) in men versus women with the same exposures to adjust the formula for the increase in cancer risk for women. Title: Does exposure to asbestos cause prostate cancer? A systematic literature review and meta-analysis
Snippet: Asbestos has been classified as the acknowledged carcinogen by International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). [34] However, whether asbestos is associated with the development of other cancers remains unknown. 

During the past 10 years, a growing body of meta-analysis has been widely used in epidemiology to quantitatively assess the association between asbestos exposure and cancers via statistical method. Numerous cohort studies and systematic reviews attempted to answer the question between asbestos exposure and PCa, however, the results were debatable. In present study, we quantitatively assessed the relationship of excessive exposure to asbestos with PCa risk by applying a meta-analysis technique based on 17 independent kinds of literature. 

Our results revealed an increased PCa risk among people exposed to asbestos. In another way, people exposed to asbestos have 1.22 times of suffering from PCa compared with the general population. The risk of PCa varied in people exposed to different type of asbestos. In subgroup analysis by asbestos type, we found a suggestive and significant association between asbestos type and the PCa in meta-SMR. Cohorts exposed to crocidolite and mixed asbestos showed larger SMRs than those exposed only to chrysotile asbestos, which is consistent with what Stayner et al [35] found for mesothelioma. In addition, the nonsignificant SMR based on the 4 cohorts with exposure to chrysotile asbestos only seems to confirm the results by Li et al, [36] which based on 3 studies. The exact mechanisms of asbestos exposure leading to PCa are not fully understood. The inherent characteristics of asbestos may affect its carcinogenicity, including fiber diameter and length, surface properties of the fiber as well as the fiber durability. Previous study has reported that the diameter of crocidolite fibers is the finest followed by chrysotile, amosite, and anthophyllite and it was considered the most harmful to human health. [8] In subgroup analysis by asbestos type, people exposed to crocidolite and mixed asbestos shows a significant association with PCa. Increased risk in PCa has also been associated with workers in a variety of dusty industries.

Title: A Meta-analysis of Asbestos and Lung Cancer: Is Better Quality Exposure Assessment Associated with Steeper Slopes of the Exposure–Response Relationships?
Snippet: For each of these studies, different measures of association were reported, most commonly standardized mortality ratios and in some cases relative risks (RRs) or odds ratios. Although there are fundamental differences between these types of risk measures, for the purpose of this metaanalysis, all study designs were included and all measures of association were considered estimates of the RR. 

The outcome analyzed in the meta-analysis was the slope of the exposure-response relation, often referred to as the "lung cancer potency factor" and denoted by K L in the asbestos literature. We used the widely applied U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (1986) linear RR model, RR = α(1 + K L × CE), where α is an intercept parameter representing the background rate of lung cancer and K L is the slope of increase in the RR per unit of CE to asbestos (in fiber-years per milliliter). If available, we used associations for 10-year lagged CE (six studies) to account for latency (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 1986); otherwise, we used associations with unlagged CE (13 studies). The values for K L were obtained by fitting Poisson regression models with PROC NLMIXED (version 9.2; SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA). In our primary analyses, we did not restrict the intercept (α) in the calculation of the exposure-response curve. Data extracted from each study to derive K L values are provided in Supplemental Material, Appendix 1 (http://dx.doi.org/10.1289/ ehp.1002879). Gustavsson et al. (2002) presented the risk estimate for their study per unit of exposure, and we derived the K L for their study using the formula provided in the paper for the RR at a cumulative dose of x fiber-years: RR = 1.494 ln(x+1) . 

The predominant fiber type each study population was exposed to was ascertained from the literature. Some populations were exposed to both chrysotile and amphiboles (including amosite, crocidolite, and tremolite) and were categorized as having experienced "mixed" exposure.

Asbestos has been classified as the acknowledged carcinogen by International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). [34] However, whether asbestos is associated with the development of other cancers remains unknown. 

During the past 10 years, a growing body of meta-analysis has been widely used in epidemiology to quantitatively assess the association between asbestos exposure and cancers via statistical method. In present study, we quantitatively assessed the relationship of excessive exposure to asbestos with PCa risk by applying a meta-analysis technique based on 17 independent kinds of literature. 

Our results revealed an increased PCa risk among people exposed to asbestos. In another way, people exposed to asbestos have 1.22 times of suffering from PCa compared with the general population. The risk of PCa varied in people exposed to different type of asbestos. In subgroup analysis by asbestos type, we found a suggestive and significant association between asbestos type and the PCa in meta-SMR. The inherent characteristics of asbestos may affect its carcinogenicity, including fiber diameter and length, surface properties of the fiber as well as the fiber durability. For each of these studies, different measures of association were reported, most commonly standardized mortality ratios and in some cases relative risks (RRs) or odds ratios. The outcome analyzed in the meta-analysis was the slope of the exposure-response relation, often referred to as the "lung cancer potency factor" and denoted by K L in the asbestos literature. We used the widely applied U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (1986) linear RR model, RR = α(1 + K L × CE), where α is an intercept parameter representing the background rate of lung cancer and K L is the slope of increase in the RR per unit of CE to asbestos (in fiber-years per milliliter). In our primary analyses, we did not restrict the intercept (α) in the calculation of the exposure-response curve. The predominant fiber type each study population was exposed to was ascertained from the literature. Some populations were exposed to both chrysotile and amphiboles (including amosite, crocidolite, and tremolite) and were categorized as having experienced "mixed" exposure.

For each of these studies, different measures of association were reported, most commonly standardized mortality ratios and in some cases relative risks (RRs) or odds ratios. Although there are fundamental differences between these types of risk measures, for the purpose of this metaanalysis, all study designs were included and all measures of association were considered estimates of the RR. 

The outcome analyzed in the meta-analysis was the slope of the exposure-response relation, often referred to as the "lung cancer potency factor" and denoted by K L in the asbestos literature. We used the widely applied U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (1986) linear RR model, RR = α(1 + K L × CE), where α is an intercept parameter representing the background rate of lung cancer and K L is the slope of increase in the RR per unit of CE to asbestos (in fiber-years per milliliter). If available, we used associations for 10-year lagged CE (six studies) to account for latency (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 1986); otherwise, we used associations with unlagged CE (13 studies). The values for K L were obtained by fitting Poisson regression models with PROC NLMIXED (version 9.2; SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA). # Summary

Epidemiological studies disagree about whether occupational asbestos exposure causes COPD in sheet metal workers because asbestos primarily induces restrictive lung injury and diffusion defects, while COPD is typically defined by persistent airflow obstruction; these outcomes are hard to separate when exposure and smoking co-occur, and both radiographic and pathologic criteria are susceptible to misclassification.<cite id="ec3dbb21-2">Asbestos exposure is associated with lower FVC and DLCO but is not significantly associated with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-4">Asbestos exposed subjects had reduced FVC, FEV1, and DLCO, but asbestos exposure alone was not significantly associated with a reduction of the FEV1/FVC</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-5">Asbestos exposure with radiographic asbestosis lowers FVC and DLCO but not FEV1/FVC; smoking further reduces DLCO and the interaction with asbestos is uncertain across studies</cite>. Cigarette smoking both confounds and interacts with asbestos, producing obstructive lung changes and altering fiber clearance, which can mask or mimic COPD among asbestos-exposed tradespeople.<cite id="ec3dbb21-2">Asbestos and smoking show additive or synergistic effects in several studies, although some report no significant interaction</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-1">Asbestos and cigarette smoke can act synergistically and both contribute to obstructive changes</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-9">Smoking can produce radiographic changes that mimic pulmonary asbestosis and is associated with interstitial fibrosis, complicating diagnosis</cite>. In sheet metal trades, exposure assessment is further complicated by overlapping exposures (e.g., fiberglass, composites), short or low-dose asbestos, and variable task histories, and outcome ascertainment often relies on self-report or insensitive tests; these factors contribute to inconsistent findings on COPD risk.<cite id="93256ebf-1">Epidemiologic studies of fiberglass exposure have generally failed to reveal chronic lung function effects</cite><cite id="93256ebf-6">Spirometric evidence of restrictive impairment was not found among nonsmoking sheet metal workers; ascertainment of pure exposure is difficult</cite><cite id="93256ebf-3">Exposure modeling in sheet metal workers relied on industrial hygienist judgments due to sparse quantitative data, with potential misclassification</cite><cite id="93256ebf-4">A high proportion of invited workers refused participation, limiting representativeness</cite><cite id="93256ebf-5">Selection bias and recall bias were concerns, and exposure models had limited validation</cite><cite id="93256ebf-9">Low respirable fiberglass exposure concentrations challenge claims of high-intensity exposure causing chronic bronchitis, underscoring exposure misclassification</cite>.

# Pathobiological Differences and Overlap

Asbestos exposure more consistently reduces total lung capacity, diffusion capacity, and sometimes DLCO than it does the FEV1/FVC ratio, which is central to COPD diagnosis.<cite id="ec3dbb21-2">Asbestos-exposed workers showed significantly reduced FVC, FEV1, and DLCO, but no significant decrease in FEV1/FVC</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-4">After adjustment, asbestos exposure was associated with restrictive dysfunction and decreased DLCO, not FEV1/FVC</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-5">Radiographic asbestosis lowers FVC and DLCO but not FEV1/FVC; smoking-associated reductions were seen in DLCO</cite>. This pattern reflects the primary pathogenesis of asbestosis—interstitial fibrosis with reduced diffusion and elastic recoil—rather than small-airway obstruction typical of COPD.<cite id="ec3dbb21-5">The mechanism of asbestos-related obstructive airway disease remains unresolved, with evidence for small airway pathology in some studies and irritant susceptibility in others</cite>. In practice, many exposed workers exhibit mixed patterns (restrictive + obstructive), which complicates attribution to a single disease process and contributes to divergent study conclusions.<cite id="ec3dbb21-2">A mixed pattern of pulmonary impairment was markedly more common among exposed subjects than controls</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-5">Smoking-asbestos workers had lower DLCO; further progression and the nature of airway involvement remain to be determined</cite>.

# Smoking as a Major Confounder and Interactor

Cigarette smoking is ubiquitous in occupational cohorts, produces obstructive lung disease, and can interact multiplicatively with asbestos to increase lung injury, making it difficult to isolate asbestos-specific COPD risk in sheet metal workers.<cite id="ec3dbb21-1">Asbestos and cigarette smoke exposure can produce obstructive changes and may act synergistically</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-2">Eleven of 21 studies reviewed showed additive or synergistic interactions between smoking and asbestos, though one reported no significant interaction</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-9">Smoking can produce radiographic and interstitial changes that mimic asbestosis and is associated with fibrosis, raising confounding concerns</cite>. In asbestos-exposed cohorts, heavy smokers often show lower DLCO and mixed impairment even when FEV1/FVC is not reduced, blurring the clinical distinction between asbestosis and COPD and leading to different conclusions depending on how outcomes are defined.<cite id="ec3dbb21-4">Smoking asbestos workers had significantly reduced DLCO compared to nonsmokers; FEV1/FVC was not significantly altered by asbestos alone</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-5">Smoking-asbestos subjects had reduced DLCO; the interaction pattern remains uncertain</cite>.

# Exposure Assessment Challenges in Sheet Metal Trades

Sheet metal work involves heterogeneous tasks and materials (e.g., chrysotile, fiberglass, composites), short or low cumulative asbestos exposure, and frequent co-exposure with welding fumes and other dusts; these factors complicate exposure classification and dose–response estimation.<cite id="93256ebf-1">Case reports and epidemiologic studies have questioned causality for fiberglass, with studies failing to show consistent radiographic or functional effects</cite><cite id="93256ebf-6">The need for very large populations and difficulty in ascertaining pure exposure are inherent challenges</cite><cite id="93256ebf-3">Exposure categories were assigned by industrial hygienist judgment due to limited industrial hygiene data; demolition scenarios may entail higher exposures than modeled tasks</cite>. Even when exposure misclassification is controlled, residual confounding by task history and co-exposures (asbestos, welding, fiberglass) can distort estimates of COPD risk.<cite id="93256ebf-5">The study design raised questions about selection bias and whether exposure models could distinguish asbestos, welding, and fibreglass exposures</cite><cite id="93256ebf-9">Low respirable fibreglass concentrations in fabrication and installation tasks argue against simple high-intensity exposure explanations, underscoring exposure uncertainty</cite>.

# Outcome Ascertainment and Diagnostic Criteria

COPD diagnosis relies on airflow obstruction that persists after bronchodilators, yet asbestos exposure can reduce DLCO and produce restrictive abnormalities or mixed patterns, which may be misclassified as COPD or asbestosis depending on testing and interpretation.<cite id="ec3dbb21-4">Asbestos exposure was associated with reduced FVC and DLCO but not FEV1/FVC</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-5">Radiographic asbestosis was associated with lower FVC and DLCO but not FEV1/FVC; mixed patterns were prominent</cite>. # Why Studies Disagree Specifically in Sheet Metal Workers

- Many sheet metal workers with potential asbestos or fiberglass exposure have short durations or low cumulative exposure, reducing detectable functional changes and increasing the likelihood of mixed or null results.<cite id="93256ebf-6">The net exposure time in the studied group corresponded to several years of handling fiberglass, with no restrictive spirometric evidence</cite><cite id="93256ebf-9">Respirable fibreglass concentrations were generally low across tasks, challenging claims of strong exposure effects</cite>.  
- Co-exposures (e.g., welding) and high smoking prevalence can drive obstructive patterns and lower DLCO, producing outcomes that do not cleanly map to COPD or asbestosis, and thus yield different conclusions depending on outcome definitions and analytic adjustments.<cite id="ec3dbb21-1">Combined asbestos and cigarette smoke exposure can promote obstructive changes</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-2">Smoking and asbestos interactions are variably observed across studies</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-4">Smoking asbestos workers had lower DLCO without a significant reduction in FEV1/FVC</cite>.  
- Exposure misclassification and selection bias are substantial in this trade, with sparse industrial hygiene data, reliance on self-reported task histories, and low response rates; these factors dilute or exaggerate associations depending on the study's design and population.<cite id="93256ebf-3">Exposure intensity categories depended on expert judgment due to limited measurements</cite><cite id="93256ebf-5">Recall bias, lack of validation of exposure models, and selection concerns were noted</cite><cite id="93256ebf-4">Low participation rates limit representativeness</cite>.

# Bottom Line

The field disagrees because asbestos exposure in sheet metal workers more often produces restrictive/diffusion abnormalities and mixed patterns, while COPD is defined by airflow obstruction; cigarette smoking—common in these cohorts—both drives obstructive changes and confounds attribution, and exposure and outcome assessments in this trade are difficult, yielding inconsistent epidemiologic findings.<cite id="ec3dbb21-2">Asbestos exposure lowers FVC/DLCO more than FEV1/FVC</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-4">Asbestos exposure was associated with restrictive dysfunction but not reduced FEV1/FVC</cite><cite id="ec3dbb21-5">Smoking further reduces DLCO and the interaction with asbestos remains uncertain</cite><cite id="93256ebf-1">Epidemiologic and functional studies of fiberglass exposure generally show no chronic effects</cite><cite id="93256ebf-6">Spirometric evidence of restrictive impairment was not found among nonsmoking sheet metal workers</cite><cite id="93256ebf-9">Low respirable fiberglass exposures and exposure misclassification challenges underscore the difficulty of detecting COPD effects</cite>.</answer>

There remains an ongoing effort to achieve ban on asbestos and the issue regarding asbestos-induced detrimental effects is still warranted to be monitored. [8][9][10] Further exploration to characterize SAO between COPD subjects with and without asbestos exposure and its underlying factors might be valuable to screen the vulnerable asbestos-exposed population.

COPD subjects are more vulnerable to ambient air pollution than healthier people, and lower lung function measurements were shown to be associated with air pollution. 11,12 There is a hypothesis implying the putative role of air pollution in modifying asbestos-related abnormalities and increasing mortality risk of asbestos-related malignant diseases, 13,14 although the possible impact of air pollution on respiratory abnormality and SAO risk among asbestos-exposed population remains largely unexplored.

It is questioned whether the exposure models are truly able to distinguish qualitatively and/or quantita- tively between the exposures of asbestos, welding, and fibreglass, given the high degree of correlation among them. No attempt was made to validate the self reported work histories (which are open to recall bias) nor to validate the models of fibreglass and asbestos exposure. More should have been done to validate the expo- sure modelling assumptions because the paper's conclusions are based on these assumptions (see industrial hygiene com- ments later). 

The overall design of the survey raises important questions about the potential impact of selection bias on the study. This includes the representativeness of the results and the validity of generalising these results beyond the sample. 

The survey's results are based on less than 40% of those eligible and invited to participate. It relied on data from a previous medical screening in which only 47% of those invited agreed to participate (12 454 of 26 329 sheet metal workers). Of this, 407 (47%) eligible workers were selected from United States Sheet Metal and Air Conditioning National Association locals in the southeast sun belt and west coast states. Only 333 (82%) of these 407 completed the interviews. 

Unanswered, yet most important ques- tions remain. How did survey eligibility criteria affect results?

We therefore decided to use only nonsmoking subjects, who constituted approximately 25 % of the total male population available for study. In order to obtain a sufficiently large number of subjects for study, all sheet metal workers in the Goteborg area who were members of the trade union were contacted (N = 522). As is obvious from table 1, the response rate was very low (47 %), in spite of our cooperation with the trade union and two additional contacts. We can only speculate about the factors guiding the individual in his decision of whether or not to participate and about the extent to which this large primary dropout influences the general applicability of the findings. One of the consequences of the low response rate and our decision to study only nonsmokers was that the number of presumptive referents was limited to 15. The group available for analysis was further reduced as a number of subjects had to be excluded because of exposure to asbestos -which has a potential effect on lung function that almost certainly outweighs the potential effect of fiber glass (3). These considerations highlight two problems inherent in every study on occupational hazards, ie, the need for a very large basic population and the difficulty in ascertaining pure exposure. 

It seems that symptoms involving the respiratory tractunrelated to occupa-tional exposure -were equally common in both our groups. On the other hand, irritation of the upper airways during heavy exposure has been reported (131, and in our exposed group six out of seven subjects claimed cough when exposed. This result may indicate that, periodically, there is a high number of airborne fibers with an aerodynamic diameter associated with deposition in the larger airways. The net time of exposure may seem rather short (table 2), but it corresponds to occupational handling of fiber glass for 6 to 10 years. 

Our study gives no spirometric evidence of the development of restrictive ventilatory impairment, a result which is in line with that of previous reports (3, 10).

Unfortunately, they did not include demoli- tion work among the tasks sampled. 

Konzen points out that, in the regression model for chronic bronchitis, years of asbestos exposure was treated as a continuous variable whereas-fibreglass exposure was treated categorically, distinguishing "high" exposure from lesser intensity expo- sures. In developing the regression models, duration of both asbestos and fibreglass exposures (all levels) were modelled in four category groups (none, low, intermediate, and high duration). Also, for fibreglass, high intensity exposure was tested for inclusion as a yes or no variable (high and medium level exposures to asbestos were too correlated to permit this.) Results for asbestos showed a monotonically increasing risk as duration increased, so we employed the sta- tistically efficient continuous variable in our final model. For fibreglass, high intensity exposure was a statistically significant pre- dictor of chronic bronchitis, whereas risk did not increase significantly with increasing duration of all fibreglass exposure. We would have liked to determine whether duration of high intensity exposure was pre- dictive of chronic bronchitis, but there was insufficient spread in the data to employ this analysis. 

Twenty eight per cent of the workers in the chronic bronchitis analysis had spent time doing fibreglass ripout (the only "high level" exposure). More than 80% of these persons with high level exposure had one or two adjusted years of high fibreglass exposure, while the remainder had up to seven adjusted years of exposure. Konzen com- ments that such fleeting exposures could not plausibly cause chronic bronchitis; in so commenting, he may not realise that .adjusted years of exposure takes into account the average % time that a sheet metal worker performed the task in question. One adjusted year of exposure could result from doing fibreglass ripout work one quarter of the time for four years, 10% time over 10 years, or 2-5% (one hour a week) over a 40 year career. These are not fleeting exposures, and in fact may represent regular perfor- mance of tasks over a lifetime of sheet metal work. 

We are pleased to have had this opportunity to respond to Konzen's criticisms.
